countingRule: F3 p005R: checkpoint number = boxes appearing up to the checkpoint incl. the C box (bracket would add Nitro; none here); C2 includes the 19 bonus boxes; steel ! blocks are listed as clusters with count 0 (not boxes)

observations: 12 of the first 17 boxes are one wall at the start: count is front-loaded and safe
on the scarab floor every crate sits on a framed solid tile: crates teach where it is safe to stand
each floor-button door or ! ride is followed within a few metres by a small reward cluster
only two clusters sit inside a hazard's firing line (S2-f light beams, P-b dart pit) - deliberate tests
three of four ! blocks move platforms; no main-route crate depends on a switch
the purple-gem course holds about a quarter of the boxes plus a secret clear gem; a visible Aku crate on the fork baits the locked door
the tar slide's momentum carries the player past two floating ? crates (return-trip count trap)
the only main-route 1UP follows the hardest timing section (pillars, moving platforms)
time trial re-reads the layout: A crates become masks so invincibility arrives exactly where a floating 3-s crate needs the big hitbox

geometryObservations: A machine stage: every stretch is built around one device — button doors, scarab tiles, a pad lift, an operator's pillar, dart lights, double doors, an extending floor, falling pillars, a tar slide, pad finales — and each is followed by a small crate receipt.

Tar is the movement verb and it is a surface, not a gap: slippery like ice (hard to stop, no dash, F3 p067L) but a slide on it is a dash and a slide-jump off it is the longest jump (TT intro). It is taught flat and walled (O-S1-a), then placed right before a pit, a pillar, spears or a hole (G-S1-b, P-S2-d, O-PURPLE-b, G-PURPLE-b).

Gaps are short (1–3 u) but almost never plain: each is coupled to a mechanism — doors (G-S1-b), a lift (G-S2-b), an extending floor (G-S3-a), a sliding floor under falling pillars (G-S3-c), dart lights (G-PURPLE-a), a switch-made bridge (G-PURPLE-c), pads (G-S4-b).

All periodic traps are timed from the start point (F3 p067L): the course is one clock, so a player who learns the cycles can flow through, and the time trial says to pass every door at its earliest opening.
Crumbling floors are read by colour: pink drops at once, green holds, framed tiles are rests — and crates sit only on framed tiles, so the crates teach the tile language (P-S2-a).

Enemies are machine operators and ambushers, not patrols: operators run the pillars and never attack, Tobigators and pot monkeys pop out of holes and pots, flamethrower workers sweep a jet, the red-eyed cobra blocks a narrow path. There is no chaser.
Ambushers debut on solid ground (pot monkeys on stairs, E-S2-a) and return on tar (E-PURPLE-a), where stopping to fight is hard: same enemy, worse footing.

Every timing gate offers a safe split: the pocket between the double doors (P-S2-f), the round pillar inside the extending-floor pit (P-S3-c), the hole edge from which the moving floor can be seen (POINT 6).

The default branch is easier than the gem branch: the purple course stacks dart lights, two tar launches, spears twice, crushers and a bridge over spikes (4 gaps, 4 hazards, 5 enemies) against the right course's machine set (3 gaps, 2 hazards, no enemies).
Both routes end with a ! that starts moving pads (G-S4-b, G-PURPLE-d), with the order announced (right, left, far) and the only big jump kept for the stairs.

The right course is built to be run both ways: F3's perfect route runs it backwards, toward the camera, where the moving floor can only be seen from the hole edge (POINT 6, POINT E) — the same geometry becomes a blind test.

Height is used sparingly and as a reward: the tar slide carries the player under two ceiling crates that need a return trip, and the bonus life ledge is reachable only from the top of a falling TNT stack (P-S4-a, P-BONUS-d).
geometryTransfer: Tar as a `slip` surface: a 6–8 m `slip` strip ending 1–2 m before a 2.3–3 m `pit`, walled on both sides, first shown with no pit at all; a slip slope (`slipGravity`) for the tar slide, with crates floating 3–4 m above it that need a walk back up. Verify how our slide and jump behave on slip floors before relying on extra distance.

Scarab walkway: a single-file 2.3 m-wide line of tiles over a `pit` — `crumble` pads with a very short `shake` (≈0.2 s) for the "pink" tiles, plain platforms of another colour for the safe ones, and a framed rest tile every 2–3 crumbles carrying the crates.

Door grammar with our primitives: the extending floor is a `mover` (axis along the route, amp ≈2 m) over a 4–6 m pit with a fixed 1.5 m pillar `platform` inside it; doors become a pair of `crusher`s on one cycle with a ≥2 m safe pocket between them; keep all cycles phased from level start so the course can be learned as one clock.
Pad finale: after the last checkpoint, three `mover` pads (2.3 m) phased to arrive right, left, far over a pit, then one 3 m jump onto stairs — the only long jump of the finale.

Light-pool trap: `firetiki` heads (or `sentry`s) covering lit floor zones across a corridor, with crates inside the zones; the counter is a slide or a diagonal path between zones. Check that our slide actually passes under the jet before using the slide-under answer.

Two-way course: build the machine stretch so it works in both directions and add `camnode`s for the reverse run; a toward-camera reverse run (`zone` N) makes a known stretch a fresh test without new geometry.
